Gradient Descent Methods
Momentum
We add a term to the update rule which helps speed up learning and avoid getting stuck in local minima of the cost function
The term we add is a factor of the previous weight change.  This has the effect of reducing the influence of the current iteration and “smoothing” training

With momentum:

Optimization Algorithms
SGD has issues:
Learning rates and schedules have to be set in advance, without knowing what may work best
Same learning rate applies to all weight updates each epoch
If our data is sparse we may want to update frequently occurring features less and rarely occurring features more
Alternatives
Adapt the learning rate to the weights
Image Source
Adagrad
Adapts the learning rate to each weight, at each time step
Lower LR (smaller updates) for weights of frequently occurring features and higher LR (larger updates) for weights of rare features
Well suited for sparse datasets (e.g. text)
Eliminates need to manually tune the LR
Weakness is that accumulated gradient in denominator eventually makes the step size too small to change weights
RMSprop
Alternative adaptive LR approach originally proposed by Geoffrey Hinton in his Coursera course
Attempt to resolve the radically diminishing learning rate in Adagrad
Adam
Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam)
Combination of the ideas behind RMSprop and momentum:
Uses both moving average of squared gradient (RMSprop) and moving average of the gradient (momentum)
Adam is generally regarded as the current “best” all-around optimizer
Other optimizers may work better for certain situations
E.g. Adagrad works very well for sparse data
Recent improvements have been made on Adam e.g. Radam, Nadam, AdamW

Challenges
Vanishing and Exploding Gradients
Getting stuck in local minima
Overfitting to training data
Long training cycles
When using activation functions like sigmoid or tanh:
These functions "squish" values into a range (0-1 for sigmoid)
Their derivatives are always less than 1 (maximum of 0.25 for sigmoid)
Vanishing Gradients
Wait, why do we care about the derivative of the activation function?
Backpropagation!
When we multiply many small numbers together during backpropagation, the result gets exponentially smaller
In a best case scenario, each layer back reduces the gradient by roughly 75% (multiplied by 0.25)
By the time we reach the early layers, the gradient is practically zero
Vanishing Gradients
Vanishing Gradients
Simplified example to understand theory:
Start at the last layer (gradient = 1.0)
Move back to previous layer
Multiply by sigmoid derivative (let’s assume maximum derivative 0.25)
Multiply by weight (let’s assume weight ~1)
New gradient = ~1*0.25 = 0.25
Move back another layer
Multiply sigmoid derivative again (<0.25)
New gradient 0.25 * 0.25 = 0.0625
Move back another layer
Multiply sigmoid derivative again (<0.25)
New gradient 0.25 * 0.0625 = 0.015625
Repeat for n layers
Vanishing Gradients
Solutions:
Use ReLU activation function
Exploding gradients occur when large numbers multiply together
Most commonly happens with:
Large weight initializations (> 1.0)
Activation functions with derivatives ≥ 1 (like ReLU)
Effects compound in deep networks
Exploding Gradients
How to spot:
Loss fluctuates widely across training cycles
Model weights become very large or go to NaN
Solutions:
Reduce mini-batch size
Use gradient clipping – limit the size of gradients
Use batch norm

Loss function ✅ (examples: MSE, binary crossentropy)
Choice of Optimization Algorithm ✅ (examples: SGD, Adam)

Regularization
Neural networks are prone to overfitting
We often use regularization techniques to reduce overfitting risk and improve convergence
Early Stopping
Image Source
The model will overfit at some point during training!
We ideally want to stop training when the validation error is at a global minimum
Good: stop when val error begins to increase
Better: stop at global minimum of val error
Best: stop at point that gives best “price-performance” ratio (optimal ratio of training time to val error)
Early Stopping
Large Learning Rate
Larger LRs help avoid getting stuck in local minima, but create risk of not converging
Has been shown that large initial LRs reduce overfitting [Source]
LR Schedules
One strategy is to start with a higher learning rate and reduce it as training progresses and the weights approach the optimum
There are many methods we can use to decay the LR
With StepLR we decay the LR every step_size epochs by a factor gamma
One-cycle LR Policy
The 1cycle LR policy cycles the LR over the training, changing it after every batch
Small initial LR increases to a set max value and then decays back down to a small value
Momentum is cycled inversely to LR to balance regularization applied
Do LR schedulers play nice with Adam?
Use of an adaptive optimizer may not be compatible with use of a learning rate scheduler
Benefits of adaptive optimizer are few/no hyperparameters to set
Benefit of LR scheduler (one-cycle policy) is potential for much quicker training (superconvergence)
In practice, try both – one-cycle policy with SGD, and Adam with no LR scheduler
Other forms of regularization can be used with adaptive optimizers:
Early stopping, weight decay, dropout, batch norm
L1 Regularization (Lasso) -
Adds a penalty equal to the absolute value of the magnitude of coefficients.
This encourages sparsity in the model (many coefficients become exactly zero).
L2 Regularization (Ridge) -
Adds a penalty equal to the square of the magnitude of coefficients.
This encourages small, but non-zero coefficients.
Regularization via loss function
Batch Normalization
In backpropagation, weights of a layer are updated under the expectation that the prior layer outputs have a given distribution
In reality the distribution shifts due to variation across batches and updates to prior layer weights (internal covariate shift)
This slows learning by requiring lower learning rates and careful initialization of weights

Dropout is when you randomly drops neurons during training to prevent overfitting.
During each training step, each neuron has a probability of being ignored. This forces the network to not rely on any specific neurons, promoting redundancy.

# Week 1: Introduction to Neural Networks  
## From Biological Neuron to Deep Learning Systems

---

## 1. Historical Foundations

### 1.1 McCulloch & Pitts Neuron (1943)

The first mathematical model of a biological neuron was proposed by **McCulloch and Pitts (1943)**.  

It models a neuron as a **weighted linear combination of inputs**:

\[
f(x, w) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i w_i
\]

Where:
- \( x_i \) = input features  
- \( w_i \) = weights  
- Output is a linear combination of inputs  

This is equivalent to **linear regression**:

\[
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \dots
\]

It represents a **linear hyperplane** decision boundary.

Initially, weights were set manually.

---

### 1.2 The Perceptron (Rosenblatt, 1958)

Rosenblatt introduced the **perceptron**, adding a **threshold (activation)**:

\[
y =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } \sum w_i x_i - T > 0 \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\]

This introduced the idea of an **activation function**, which:
- Converts weighted sum into a decision
- Acts as a binary classifier

However:

> A single perceptron can only learn **linear decision boundaries**.

Thus, problems like **non-linearly separable data (e.g., XOR)** cannot be solved with a single neuron.

---

## 2. Multilayer Perceptron (MLP)

Adding hidden layers introduces **nonlinearity**.

Structure:
- **Input layer**
- **Hidden layer(s)**
- **Output layer**

Example hidden neuron:

\[
z^{(2)}_1 = w^{(2)}_{1,1}x_1 + w^{(2)}_{2,1}x_2 + w^{(2)}_{3,1}x_3 + b^{(2)}_1
\]

\[
a^{(2)}_1 = \Phi(z^{(2)}_1)
\]

Where:
- \( \Phi \) = activation function
- \( b \) = bias term

### Universal Approximation Theorem

With sufficiently many hidden units, an MLP can approximate **any function**.

Stacking linear units + nonlinear activations enables modeling **nonlinear decision boundaries**.

---

## 3. Evolution of Neural Networks

### Timeline Highlights

- **1943** – McCulloch & Pitts neuron  
- **1958** – Perceptron  
- **1982** – Hopfield networks  
- **1986** – Backpropagation rediscovered  
- **2009** – ImageNet (Fei-Fei Li)  
- **2012** – AlexNet (CNN breakthrough)  
- **2015** – ResNet  
- **2017** – *Attention is All You Need* (Transformers)  
- **2022** – ChatGPT (Generative AI boom)

Periods of low funding are known as **AI Winters**.

---

## 4. Why Deep Learning Now?

Three major drivers:

### 4.1 Data Availability
- Massive labeled datasets (e.g., ImageNet: 1.2M images)
- Sensors, internet-scale data
- Crowdsourced labeling (e.g., Mechanical Turk)

### 4.2 Computational Power
- GPUs
- Cloud infrastructure
- Exponential growth in compute

### 4.3 Algorithmic Advances
- Backpropagation
- CNNs
- Transformers
- Improved optimizers

---

## 5. When to Use Neural Networks

Neural networks are appropriate when:

- Large training datasets available  
- High-dimensional or unstructured data (images, text)  
- Complex nonlinear relationships  
- Low need for interpretability  

---

## 6. Limitations of Neural Networks

- Computationally expensive  
- Power-hungry  
- Non-convex optimization  
- Difficult to interpret  
- High overfitting risk  

Example:  
A small 28×28 image with 3 layers can require:

\[
28 \times 28 \times 100 \times 10 = 784,000 \text{ weights}
\]

---

## 7. Deep Learning

“Deep” refers to **number of layers**.

More layers → hierarchical feature learning:
- Early layers: simple features
- Deeper layers: abstract features

Deep learning:
- Automatically learns features
- Excels in:
  - Computer Vision
  - NLP
  - Generative modeling

---

## 8. Activation Functions

### Purpose
- Introduce **nonlinearity**
- Control output range
- Decide signal propagation

### Common Activation Functions

#### **Sigmoid**
\[
\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}
\]
- Range: (0,1)
- Used in binary classification output
- Suffers from vanishing gradients

#### **Tanh**
- Range: (-1,1)
- Zero-centered
- Still vanishing gradient issue

#### **ReLU**
\[
\text{ReLU}(z) = \max(0,z)
\]
- Efficient
- Default for hidden layers
- Avoids vanishing gradients (mostly)

#### **Leaky ReLU**
- Small slope for negative inputs
- Prevents “dying ReLU”

#### **Softmax**
\[
\text{Softmax}(z_i) = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}
\]
- Outputs probability distribution
- Used in multi-class classification

---

## 9. Bias Term

Bias allows shifting the activation function:

\[
z = w^T x + b
\]

Without bias:
- Only scaling possible  
With bias:
- Shift decision boundary  

Bias is a **learnable parameter**.

---

## 10. Training a Neural Network

### Step 1: Initialize
- Small random weights

### Step 2: Forward Pass
- Compute predictions

### Step 3: Compute Loss

Example (Regression):
- Mean Absolute Error (MAE):
\[
L = |y - \hat{y}|
\]
- Mean Squared Error (MSE):
\[
L = (y - \hat{y})^2
\]

### Loss vs Cost
- **Loss**: error per example  
- **Cost**: average loss across dataset  

### Classification Loss
- Binary Cross Entropy
- Categorical Cross Entropy

---

## 11. Backpropagation

Goal: Compute gradient of loss w.r.t. each parameter.

Uses **chain rule**:

\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial w}
\]

General result:

\[
\frac{\partial J}{\partial w_{ij}^{(l)}} = \delta_j^{(l)} a_i^{(l-1)}
\]

Where:
- \( \delta \) = error term
- \( a \) = activation

---

## 12. Gradient Descent

Update rule:

\[
w_{j}^{(t+1)} = w_{j}^{(t)} - \eta \frac{\partial J}{\partial w_j}
\]

Where:
- \( \eta \) = learning rate

### Learning Rate Effects
- Too small → slow convergence
- Too large → divergence
- Optimal → fast, stable convergence

Typical range:
\[
0.001 \text{ to } 0.01
\]

---

## 13. Optimization Algorithms

### SGD
- Updates per sample
- Noisy but useful for online learning

### Momentum
- Adds previous update term
- Smooths training

### Adagrad
- Adaptive per-parameter learning rate
- Good for sparse data
- Learning rate shrinks too much over time

### RMSprop
- Exponential moving average of squared gradients

### Adam
Combines:
- Momentum
- RMSprop

Most widely used optimizer.

Variants:
- AdamW
- RAdam
- Nadam

---

## 14. Training Challenges

### 14.1 Vanishing Gradients

Occurs when:
- Using sigmoid/tanh
- Gradients < 1 repeatedly multiplied

Example:
\[
0.25^n \rightarrow 0
\]

Solution:
- Use ReLU in hidden layers

---

### 14.2 Exploding Gradients

Occurs when:
- Large weights
- Deep networks

Symptoms:
- Loss fluctuates wildly
- Weights become very large or NaN

Solutions:
- Gradient clipping
- Smaller batch size
- Batch normalization

---

## 15. Data Splitting

Three sets:

- **Training set**
- **Validation set**
- **Test set**

Rules:
- Test set used only once at final evaluation
- Same test set across models

---

## 16. Regularization Techniques

### Early Stopping
Stop training when validation error increases.

### Learning Rate Schedules
- StepLR
- One-cycle policy

### L1 Regularization (Lasso)
\[
\lambda \sum |w|
\]
Encourages sparsity.

### L2 Regularization (Ridge)
\[
\lambda \sum w^2
\]
Encourages small weights.

### Batch Normalization
- Normalizes layer inputs
- Stabilizes training
- Learnable scale + shift parameters

### Dropout
- Randomly disables neurons
- Prevents co-adaptation
- Reduces overfitting

---

# 5-Minute Exercise: Learning Rate Tuning

### Objective
Observe effect of learning rate on convergence.

### Setup
Train a small neural network (e.g., 2-layer MLP) on simple dataset.

### Experiment 1 — Too Small LR
- Set \( \eta = 0.00001 \)
- Observe:
  - Very slow loss decrease
  - Many epochs required

### Experiment 2 — Too Large LR
- Set \( \eta = 1.0 \)
- Observe:
  - Loss oscillates or diverges
  - May produce NaN

### Experiment 3 — Good LR
- Set \( \eta = 0.01 \)
- Observe:
  - Smooth convergence
  - Stable loss reduction

### Discussion Questions
1. What does divergence look like in the loss curve?
2. How can you detect exploding gradients early?
3. Why might Adam be more stable than SGD?
4. For counting blueberries (regression), which loss function would you choose and why?
5. When would SGD + one-cycle outperform Adam?

---

# Summary

This lecture covered:

- Evolution from linear neuron → perceptron → multilayer perceptron  
- Universal approximation and nonlinearity  
- Activation functions and bias  
- Forward pass, loss functions, backpropagation  
- Gradient descent and learning rate sensitivity  
- Modern optimizers (Adam)  
- Training challenges (vanishing/exploding gradients)  
- Regularization and generalization strategies  

Neural networks combine:
- Linear algebra
- Calculus (chain rule)
- Optimization
- Large-scale computation

They remain powerful but require careful tuning, sufficient data, and thoughtful regularization.

CNN Pipeline
Here is the standard architectural flow used in the Inception-v3 model from your research:
Image Input: The raw pixel grid (e.g., $224 \times 224 \times 3$ for color).
Convolution Layer: A kernel/filter slides over the image to extract features like edges or textures.
Activation (ReLU): This is applied immediately after each convolution to introduce non-linearity by turning negative values to zero.
Pooling Layer: Reduces the spatial dimensions (width and height) of the feature maps to save on computation.
Repeat: Multiple "Convolution + ReLU + Pooling" stages (like the Inception modules) are stacked to find complex shapes like eyes or mouths.
Final Feature Map: The high-level features extracted by the deep layers.
Flattening: This layer converts the 2D/3D feature maps into a 1D vector (a long list of numbers).
Fully Connected (Dense) Layer: Acts like a traditional neural network where every input is connected to every output to "reason" about the features.
Softmax: The final activation function that turns the output into probabilities (e.g., 90% Happy, 5% Neutral, 5% Sad).
Output Classification: The final decision (Positive, Negative, or Neutral).

# Computer Vision I — Foundations of CNNs and Modern Practice

## 1. Introduction to Computer Vision

### 1.1 Core Tasks in Computer Vision

Computer vision (CV) concerns automated understanding of images and videos. Major task categories include:

- **Image Classification**: Assign a single label to an image (e.g., dog vs. cat).
- **Object Detection**: Detect and localize objects using **bounding boxes**.
- **Image Segmentation**:
  - **Semantic segmentation**: Assign a class to each pixel.
  - **Instance segmentation**: Separate individual object instances.
  - **Object masking**: Identify object regions precisely.
- **Keypoint Detection**: Detect landmark points (e.g., joints in pose estimation).
- **Object Tracking / Motion Analysis**
- **Scene Reconstruction** (3D modeling, AR/VR)

### 1.2 Application Areas

- **Autonomous driving**
- **Medical imaging** (region-of-interest detection)
- **Manufacturing & agriculture**
- **Surveillance & sports analytics**
- **Facial recognition & product identification**

---

## 2. Challenges in Computer Vision

Real-world image data is complex and noisy:

- **Occlusion** (objects partially hidden)
- **Lighting variation**
- **Background clutter**
- **Pose & perspective changes**
- **Scale variation**
- **Ambiguity in depth/spatial reasoning**

Additional constraints:

- Need for **very large labeled datasets**
- Requirement for **fast inference** (e.g., real-time systems)
- Deployment mismatch between curated training data and messy real-world data

---

## 3. Image Representation

An image is a tensor:

- Dimensions: **H × W × C**
  - Example: `1080 × 1920 × 3`
- Each pixel contains **three channels (RGB)**:
  - Example: `[214, 197, 205]`

Thus, images are large high-dimensional arrays.

---

# 4. Traditional Computer Vision

Before deep learning, CV relied on **manual feature engineering** followed by classical ML models.

## 4.1 Handcrafted Feature Types

### 4.1.1 Color-Based Features

- **Color Histograms**
- **Color Moments** (mean, standard deviation, skewness)
- **Dominant Colors** (via clustering, e.g., k-means)
- **Color Coherence Vectors** (spatial awareness of color regions)

---

### 4.1.2 Texture-Based Features

Capture spatial relationships of pixel intensities:

- **GLCM (Gray Level Co-occurrence Matrix)**
  - Derived metrics: contrast, correlation, entropy
- **Local Binary Patterns (LBP)**
- **Gabor Filters**
- **Haralick Features**

Applications: fingerprint recognition, MRI/CT analysis, surface inspection.

---

### 4.1.3 Statistical Features

- Mean, variance, standard deviation
- **Entropy** (image complexity)
- **Zernike Moments** (rotation-invariant descriptors)
- **Wavelet Transforms** (multi-scale analysis)

---

### 4.1.4 Shape Features

- **Edge Detection**: Sobel, Canny, Prewitt
- **Contour Descriptors**
- **Hu Moments** (invariant to rotation, scale, translation)
- **SIFT / SURF** (keypoint detection, transformation robustness)
- **HOG (Histogram of Oriented Gradients)**

---

## 4.2 Classical ML Models

Used after feature extraction:

- **SVM** (high-dimensional classification)
- **Random Forest**
- **Gradient Boosting / XGBoost**
- **k-NN**
- **Decision Trees**

---

## 4.3 Limitations of Traditional CV

- Requires **domain expertise**
- Loses spatial relationships
- Cannot model **hierarchical patterns**
- Poor generalization
- High-dimensional feature vectors
- Expensive at high resolutions

This motivates **deep learning**.

---

# 5. Neural Networks for Images

## 5.1 Fully Connected Networks Are Inefficient

Example:

Input: `228 × 228 × 3`

Flattened size:
\[
228 \times 228 \times 3 = 155,952
\]

If connected to 10 neurons:
\[
155,952 \times 10 + 10 = 1,559,530 \text{ parameters}
\]

This is inefficient and ignores spatial locality.

---

# 6. Convolution

## 6.1 Intuition

Convolution is a **sliding window operation**:

- A **kernel/filter** slides across input.
- At each position, compute a **weighted sum**.

---

## 6.2 1D Convolution

For time-series:
\[
y[i] = \sum_k x[i+k] \cdot w[k]
\]

Used for signals.

---

## 6.3 2D Convolution (Images)

Kernel slides across width and height:

\[
\text{Output}(i,j) = \sum_{m,n} X(i+m,j+n) \cdot W(m,n)
\]

---

## 6.4 3D Convolution

For videos or volumetric data:

- Convolution across width, height, and depth/time.

---

# 7. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)

## 7.1 Key Ideas

- **Local connectivity** (receptive fields)
- **Weight sharing**
- **Translation invariance**
- Dramatic reduction in parameters

Example:

Filter size: `3 × 3 × 3`, 10 filters:

\[
3 \times 3 \times 3 \times 10 + 10 = 280 \text{ parameters}
\]

vs. 1.5 million in fully connected layer.

---

## 7.2 CNN Components

### 7.2.1 Convolutional Layer

- Filters of size \( F \times F \times D \)
- Output: **Feature maps**
- Each filter learns specific patterns

---

### 7.2.2 Stride (S)

- Number of pixels the filter moves per step.
- Larger stride → downsampling.

---

### 7.2.3 Padding (P)

Adds zeros around borders.

Output size formula:

\[
\text{Output} = \frac{W - F + 2P}{S} + 1
\]

“Same” convolution:
\[
P = \frac{F - 1}{2}
\]

---

### 7.2.4 Pooling Layer

Downsampling operation:

- **Max pooling** (most common)
- **Average pooling**

Typically:

- Filter: `2 × 2`
- Stride: `2`

Benefits:

- Reduces computation
- Provides spatial invariance
- Acts as regularization

---

## 7.3 Canonical CNN Pipeline

\[
\text{Conv} \rightarrow \text{BatchNorm} \rightarrow \text{ReLU} \rightarrow \text{Pooling}
\]

Repeat multiple times.

Then:

\[
\text{Flatten} \rightarrow \text{Fully Connected} \rightarrow \text{Softmax}
\]

---

# 8. CNN Architectures

## 8.1 LeNet (1990s)

- First successful CNN.
- Used for digit recognition.

---

## 8.2 AlexNet (2012)

- ImageNet breakthrough.
- Much deeper than LeNet.
- Popularized CNNs.

---

## 8.3 VGGNet (2014)

- Stacked **3×3 convolutions**
- Deep but homogeneous architecture.
- Showed small filters outperform large ones.

---

## 8.4 Accuracy Saturation Problem

Deeper plain networks:

- Training error increases
- Optimization becomes difficult
- Not overfitting — optimization failure

---

## 8.5 ResNet

Introduced **skip connections**:

\[
y = F(x) + x
\]

Benefits:

- Enables identity mapping
- Improves gradient flow
- Solves vanishing gradient
- Enables very deep networks (50, 101, 152 layers)

---

## 8.6 Inception

Parallel convolutions:

- 1×1
- 3×3
- 5×5
- Max pooling

Concatenate outputs.

Advantages:

- Multi-scale feature extraction
- Parameter efficiency
- State-of-the-art in 2014

---

# 9. Transfer Learning

Most modern CV uses pretrained models.

## 9.1 Feature Extraction

- Use pretrained backbone (e.g., ResNet on ImageNet)
- Remove final layer
- Add custom classification head
- Freeze backbone weights

---

## 9.2 Fine-Tuning

- Start with pretrained weights
- Unfreeze some/all layers
- Use smaller learning rate
- Train for fewer epochs

---

# 10. Data Augmentation

Improves robustness.

Apply **only to training data**.

Common transforms:

- Random cropping
- Rotation
- Horizontal flipping
- Brightness/saturation jitter
- Scaling

In:

- **PyTorch**: `transforms` + `ImageFolder`
- **TensorFlow**: `ImageDataGenerator`

Each epoch sees new augmented samples.

---

# 11. Implementation Notes

## 11.1 Output Size Example

Given:

- \( W = 28 \)
- \( F = 3 \)
- \( P = 0 \)
- \( S = 1 \)

\[
\frac{28 - 3 + 2(0)}{1} + 1 = 26
\]

Pooling:

\[
\frac{26 - 2}{2} + 1 = 13
\]

Flatten example:

\[
5 \times 5 \times 20 = 500
\]

---

## 11.2 Practical Workflow

1. Choose pretrained backbone (ResNet/VGG/Inception)
2. Apply transfer learning
3. Add thoughtful data augmentation
4. Evaluate generalization
5. Iterate architecture if needed

---

# Summary of Key Concepts

- Traditional CV relied on **manual feature engineering**.
- CNNs use **local receptive fields + shared weights**.
- Convolution reduces parameters dramatically.
- Pooling enables spatial invariance.
- Deep networks require architectural innovations (ResNet).
- Modern practice relies heavily on **transfer learning**.
- Data augmentation improves robustness to real-world variation.
- Architecture design balances **accuracy vs. computational cost**.

Vision Transformers (ViT)
Paper, 2021
“Visual tokens”  → word tokens
Images are divided into fixed-size patches (typically 16x16 pixels)
Each patch is flattened into a 1D vector and linearly embedded
Position embeddings are added to maintain spatial information
Vision Transformers (ViT)
Paper, 2021

Multi-head self-attention to capture relationships between patches
MLP blocks with GELU activation
Layer normalization and residual connections
Vision Transformers (ViT)
Paper, 2021
Multi Head Attention - what it allows
Each patch can attend to (pay attention to) all other patches in the image
Attention weights reveal which parts of the image are relevant for the model's decisions
Multiple attention heads learn different types of relationships between patches
Vision Transformers (ViT)
Paper, 2021
Advantages:
Global receptive field from the start
Strong performance on large datasets
More flexible architecture for multi-modal tasks
Challenges:
Computationally intensive for high-resolution images
Requires large datasets for training
May miss fine-grained local features that CNNs naturally capture

# Lecture 3 – Computer Vision II

- **Applied Computer Vision**
  - Image Classification

# 1. Applied Computer Vision

## 1.1 Image Classification

### Task Definition

Image classification assigns a **single class label** to an entire image.

**Input:**
- Image of shape `H × W × 3` (RGB)
- Pixel values typically in `[0, 255]`, normalized before training

**Output:**
- Probability vector of size `C` (number of classes)
- Produced via **softmax**
  
Example:
- Dog: 0.82
- Cat: 0.11
- Bear: 0.06
- Bird: 0.01


### Real-World Applications

- **Domino’s Pizza Quality Scanner**
- **Google Dermatology Assist**
  
These systems use classification to automate quality control and diagnosis.

---

## 1.2 Classification Architectures

Previously discussed:
- **AlexNet**
- **VGG (11, 13, 16, 19)**
- **ResNet (18, 34, 101, 152)**
- **Inception v3**

New models introduced:

---

### DenseNet

**Core Idea:**  
Each layer connects to **every previous layer** via concatenation.

If there are `L` layers:
\[
\frac{L(L+1)}{2}
\]
direct connections.

**Mechanism:**
- Feature maps are **concatenated**, not added (unlike ResNet).
- Encourages **feature reuse**.

**Pros:**
- Alleviates vanishing gradient
- Strong feature propagation
- Improved information flow

**Cons:**
- High memory usage
- Complex and harder to tune

---

### SqueezeNet

Designed for **parameter efficiency**.

**Architecture:**
- **Squeeze layer:** 1×1 convolutions (reduces channel depth)
- **Expand layer:** mix of 1×1 and 3×3 convolutions

**Advantages:**
- Significantly fewer parameters
- Lower computation cost
- Similar idea to Inception modules

---

## 1.3 Pre-Trained (Foundation) Models

A **pre-trained model**:
- Trained on a large dataset (e.g., ImageNet)
- Used as a starting point for new tasks
- Often called a **foundation model**

Available in:
- PyTorch Model Zoo
- TensorFlow Model Garden

---

### Transfer Learning Workflow

1. **Load pre-trained model**
2. **Freeze weights** (disable autograd)
3. **Replace final fully connected layer**
4. Train only new classification head
5. Optionally:
   - Unfreeze some or all layers
   - Fine-tune entire model

Benefits:
- Faster convergence
- Less data required
- Lower compute cost

---

# 2. Object Detection

## Why Detection Instead of Classification?

- **Explainability**: shows where object is
- **Autonomy**: spatial awareness required for robotics, driving, etc.

---

## 2.1 Bounding Boxes

Each detection includes:

```python
{
 'bbox': [x, y, width, height],  # normalized [0,1]
 'class_id': 2,
 'confidence': 0.98
}
```
Alternate formats:

- `[x_min, y_min, x_max, y_max]`
- Separate lists for:
  - Bounding boxes
  - Class IDs
  - Confidence scores

---

## COCO Annotation Standard

The **COCO (Common Objects in Context)** dataset defines a widely used bounding box format:

\[
\text{bbox} = [x_{\text{top-left}}, y_{\text{top-left}}, \text{width}, \text{height}]
\]

Where:
- \( x, y \) are the **top-left coordinates**
- Width and height define box dimensions
- Values are often normalized to \([0,1]\)

COCO dataset statistics:
- >200,000 labeled images
- ~1.5 million object instances
- 80 object categories

Most modern detection models are pre-trained on COCO.

---

# Anchor Boxes

## Motivation

Objects vary in:
- Scale
- Aspect ratio
- Location

Instead of predicting arbitrary boxes directly, models use **anchor boxes**:
- Predefined boxes of various sizes and shapes
- Placed across the image grid
- Each anchor predicts:
  - Offset adjustments
  - Class
  - Confidence score

Anchor box sizes can:
- Be manually defined
- Be learned from training data

Large objects → larger anchors  
Small objects → smaller anchors

---

# Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)

Because many anchors overlap:

1. Remove boxes with confidence below threshold.
2. Compute **Intersection over Union (IoU)** between overlapping boxes.
3. If IoU exceeds threshold:
   - Keep higher-confidence box
   - Suppress the other

---

## Intersection over Union (IoU)

\[
IoU = \frac{\text{Area of Overlap}}{\text{Area of Union}}
\]

- IoU close to 1 → high overlap (good detection)
- IoU close to 0 → poor alignment

IoU is used both:
- During evaluation
- During NMS

---

# YOLO (You Only Look Once)

## Core Concept

- Divide image into \( S \times S \) grid.
- Each grid cell predicts:
  - \( N \) bounding boxes
  - Class probabilities
  - Objectness score

Total predictions:
\[
S \times S \times N
\]

---

## YOLOv3 Details

- Uses **9 anchor boxes**
- Predicts offsets from anchor:
  - Center location within grid cell
  - Width adjustment
  - Height adjustment
- Also predicts class probabilities
- Backbone: **Darknet-53**
- Emphasizes fast, near real-time inference

Primary advantage:
- High speed with competitive accuracy

---

# R-CNN Family

## R-CNN

Pipeline:
1. Generate ~2000 region proposals (Selective Search)
2. Warp each region to fixed size
3. Extract CNN features (e.g., AlexNet)
4. Classify using SVM
5. Refine boxes via regression

Issues:
- Very slow (~47s per image)
- Requires feature caching
- Multi-stage training

---

## Faster R-CNN

Improvements:
- Replace selective search with **Region Proposal Network (RPN)**
- Compute feature map once per image
- Use **RoI Pooling** to extract region features
- End-to-end training via multi-task loss

Performance:
- ~0.2 seconds per image
- Eliminates feature caching

---

# Semantic Segmentation

## Definition

Assign a class label to **every pixel** in the image.

Output shape:
\[
H \times W \times 1
\]

---

## Instance Segmentation

Difference from semantic segmentation:

- Semantic: labels all pixels of same class identically
- Instance: distinguishes different objects of same class

Output:
- List of masks
- Each mask has:
  - Binary pixel map
  - Class ID
  - Confidence score

---

# U-Net Architecture

Designed for semantic segmentation.

## Encoder (Contracting Path)

- Convolution layers
- Max pooling
- Reduces spatial resolution
- Increases feature depth

## Decoder (Expanding Path)

- Upsampling
- Convolution layers
- Restores spatial resolution

## Skip Connections

- Concatenate encoder feature maps to decoder layers
- Preserve fine-grained spatial information

## Final Layer

- 1×1 convolution
- Pixel-wise softmax
- Produces per-class probability map

Other segmentation models:
- Mask R-CNN
- DeepLabV3+
- PSPNet
- SegNet

---

# Model Evaluation

## Classification Metrics

- **Accuracy**
\[
\frac{\text{Correct Predictions}}{\text{Total Predictions}}
\]

- **Precision**
\[
\frac{TP}{TP + FP}
\]

- **Recall**
\[
\frac{TP}{TP + FN}
\]

- **F1 Score**
\[
2 \cdot \frac{Precision \cdot Recall}{Precision + Recall}
\]

- AUC-ROC
- Confusion Matrix

Best practices:
- Stratified splits
- Per-class reporting
- Top-k accuracy (large class sets)
- Cross-validation (small datasets)

---

# Object Detection Evaluation

## Mean Average Precision (mAP)

Procedure:

1. Compute IoU for each predicted box.
2. Set IoU threshold (e.g., 0.5).
3. Classify predictions as TP or FP.
4. Build Precision–Recall curve.
5. Compute area under curve → Average Precision (AP).
6. Average AP across classes → mAP.

Common metrics:
- mAP@0.5
- mAP@0.75
- COCO mAP (0.5–0.95 averaged)

---

# Segmentation Evaluation

- **Mean IoU (mIoU)**
- Pixel Accuracy
- Mean Pixel Accuracy
- Frequency-weighted IoU
- Boundary F1 Score

Best practices:
- Report per-class IoU
- Evaluate small/medium/large objects separately

---

# General Evaluation Best Practices

- Qualitative failure analysis
- Visualization of predictions
- Evaluate under different conditions:
  - Lighting
  - Scale
  - Occlusion
- Report:
  - Inference time
  - Parameter count
  - FLOPs
  - Memory usage

Per-class metrics often reveal dataset bias.

---

# Advanced Topics

## Vision Transformers (ViT)

### Key Idea

- Split image into 16×16 patches.
- Flatten patches → tokens.
- Add positional embeddings.
- Feed into transformer encoder.

Architecture:
- Multi-head self-attention
- MLP with GELU activation
- Layer normalization
- Residual connections

Advantages:
- Global receptive field
- Multimodal flexibility

Challenges:
- High compute cost
- Large data requirement
- May miss fine local detail

Applications:
- Classification
- Detection
- Segmentation
- Generation
- Video understanding

---

# Grounding DINO + SAM

## Grounding DINO

- Zero-shot object detection
- Vision-language fusion
- Detect unseen objects via text prompts

## Segment Anything Model (SAM)

- ViT image encoder
- Prompt encoder

# Diffusion Models

Image generation via iterative **denoising**.

### Forward Process
Gradually add Gaussian noise.

### Reverse Process
Train model to remove noise step-by-step.

\[
x_{t-1} = \text{Denoise}(x_t)
\]

## Text-Conditioned Diffusion

- Encode text prompt.
- Inject via cross-attention into U-Net.
- Guide denoising toward desired image.

Examples:
- Stable Diffusion
- DALL·E

Latent diffusion:
- Operates in compressed latent space
- More computationally efficient

Neural networks require fixed-size inputs for efficient computation and batching. Since text sequences vary in length, they must be padded or packed to ensure consistent tensor dimensions. Without this, batching and parallel processing would not be possible.

Computers work with matrices.
If one sentence has 5 words and another has 12, you can’t stack them into the same matrix unless you pad the shorter one.
❓ What are the two main solutions?
✅ Model Answer
The two main approaches are padding and packed sequences. Padding adds special tokens (e.g., <PAD>) to shorter sequences, while packed sequences allow frameworks like PyTorch to process only valid time steps without computing over padding.

In imbalanced datasets, models tend to favor the majority class, leading to poor performance on minority classes. This results in misleading accuracy scores and poor real-world generalization.

✅ Model Answer
Full fine-tuning updates all model parameters, while frozen backbone training keeps pretrained layers fixed and only trains task-specific layers. Freezing reduces overfitting and computational cost.
❓ What is gradual unfreezing?
✅ Model Answer
Gradual unfreezing involves training the final layer first, then progressively unfreezing earlier layers. This prevents sudden disruption of pretrained weights and stabilizes training.

nlp hard why?
- text ≠ images. images = pixel rgb vals easy
- words have diff meanings depending on context (polysemy)
"bank" = river bank OR money bank
"sick" = ill OR slang 4 cool (no cap lol)
- synonyms = same meaning diff word
sneakers / tennis shoes / running shoes all = same thing
- observations NOT independent!! history matters
"dog ate the bone. it tasted good" - what is "it"??
cant understand "it" w/o prev sentence -> context dependency
"i saw boy on beach w/ binoculars" -> whos binoculars??
this "it" dependency thing is why RNNs were invented, remember for exam
SEARCH
- google bing etc all use nlp under hood
- query understanding = nlp
MACHINE TRANSLATION
- google translate, deepl etc
- seq2seq problem
TEXT CLASSIFICATION
- spam detection (email filter)
- article sorting/tagging
SENTIMENT ANALYSIS
- market research, social media monitoring, product reviews
- ex: amazon reviews -> pos/neg/neutral
TEXT SIMILARITY
- plagiarism detection (grammarly etc)
- doc dedup
TOPIC MODELING
- auto-tag web articles
- tag product review attributes
- unsupervised!!
Q&A + CHATBOTS
- rule based (old) vs RAG based (new)
- chatgpt = text gen not strict Q&A
TEXT SUMMARIZATION
- amazon review summaries = abstractive summ
- 2 types: extractive (copy sentences) vs abstractive (gen new text)
TEXT GENERATION
- chatgpt gemini claude = all this
MULTIMODAL
- NLP + vision combined
- CLIP, GPT4V etc
- "NLP plus" per prof lol
one-hot encoding (OLD SCHOOL, BAD):
- vocab size = V
- each word = vector of len V w/ 1 in its position, 0 everywhere else
- "cat" = [0,0,1,0,0....0]
- PROBLEMS:
* HUGE sparse vectors (vocab = 50k? = 50k dim vector)
* NO semantic meaning (cat vs kitten as different as cat vs nuclear)
* no relationship between words captured at all
BAG OF WORDS (BoW):
- represent whole doc as word freq counts
- vocab = all unique words across corpus
- doc = vector of counts for each vocab word
- "the cat sat" -> {the:1, cat:1, sat:1, dog:0, ran:0...}
- ignores ORDER completely!! grammar gone
- sparse (most vals = 0)
- still widely used for baseline stuff
TF-IDF (better than BoW):
TF = count of word in doc / total words in doc
IDF = log(N / df_t)
N = # total docs in corpus
df_t = # docs that contain term t
TF-IDF score = TF * IDF
intuition:
- word in EVERY doc (like "the") -> high TF, very low IDF -> low score (good, penalized)
- word in FEW docs but appears often in THIS doc -> high TF, high IDF -> high score (good, rewarded)
- rewards rare-but-specific terms, punishes stopwords
>>>> ADV: prof said TF-IDF was invented in 2012 by the word2vec team at google as a precursor to neural embeddings. this is the main reason we still use it today.
N-GRAMS:
- unigram = single word
- bigram = 2 consecutive words
- trigram = 3 consecutive words
- "machine learning is cool" -> bigrams: [machine learning], [learning is], [is cool]
- captures LOCAL context unlike pure BoW
- but combinatorial explosion as n grows
- sparsity gets worse w/ higher n
example: bigram for sentiment
"not good" = DIFFERENT from "good" (BoW cant tell diff, bigram can)
use case: find most relevant lecture note given a query
step 1: vectorize all docs w/ TfidfVectorizer
step 2: vectorize query same way
step 3: cosine_sim = dot(A, B) / (||A|| * ||B||)
- 1.0 = identical, 0.0 = totally diff
step 4: return doc w/ highest cosine sim to query
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity
import numpy as np
docs = ["deep learning uses backprop", "NLP uses transformers", "RNNs process sequences"]
query = ["sequence model"]
vec = TfidfVectorizer()
X = vec.fit_transform(docs)
q = vec.transform(query)
sims = cosine_similarity(q, X)  # shape (1, n_docs)
best = np.argmax(sims)
# returns index of most similar doc
this = basically original retrieval before neural search
dense retrieval (like FAISS + BERT embeds) = modern version of this
"the OG RAG before RAG was RAG" - my words not profs lmao
ORDER MATTERS (usually):
1. lowercasing (Running -> running)
2. punct removal (hello, world! -> hello world)
3. tokenization (split into tokens)
4. stopword removal (remove "the", "a", "is"...)
5. stemming OR lemmatization
TOKENIZATION:
word-level:
"I love NLP" -> ["I", "love", "NLP"]
simple but fails on OOV words (out of vocab)
subword (BPE - byte pair encoding):
learns common subwords from corpus
"unhappiness" -> ["un", "happy", "ness"] or ["un", "happiness"]
handles OOV!! bc even new words have known subwords
used in GPT, BERT etc
GPT-2 vocab = ~50k subword tokens
char-level:
split into individual chars
["I"," ","l","o","v","e"," ","N","L","P"]
handles ANYTHING but long sequences + no semantic meaning per char
>>>> ADV: word-level tokenization is used in all modern transformers including BERT and GPT because it is computationally most efficient.
STOPWORDS:
- common words w/ little semantic content
- "the" "is" "a" "of" "and" etc
- sklearn + nltk have lists
- WARNING: sometimes removing stopwords HURTS
"not good" -> remove "not" -> "good" -> WRONG SENTIMENT
depends on task!!
STEMMING vs LEMMATIZATION:
stemming (fast, crude):

# Natural Language Processing I — Week 6

## 1. Overview of Natural Language Processing (NLP)

### 1.1 Definition
**Natural Language Processing (NLP)** is the field of artificial intelligence concerned with enabling machines to understand, represent, generate, and reason over human language.

Unlike images (which are naturally represented as pixel intensity matrices), text must be transformed into numerical representations before being processed by machine learning models.

---

## 2. NLP Tasks and Applications

### 2.1 Core Applications

- **Search Engines**
  - Query understanding
  - Document retrieval and ranking
  - Examples: Google, Bing

- **Machine Translation**
  - Sequence-to-sequence mapping
  - Examples: Google Translate, DeepL

- **Text Classification**
  - Spam detection
  - Article tagging
  - Intent classification

- **Sentiment Analysis**
  - Product reviews (positive/negative/neutral)
  - Market research
  - Social media monitoring

- **Text Similarity**
  - Plagiarism detection
  - Document deduplication
  - Retrieval systems

- **Topic Modeling**
  - Automatic tagging of documents
  - Attribute extraction
  - Typically unsupervised

- **Question Answering (Q&A) and Chatbots**
  - Rule-based systems (legacy)
  - Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
  - Generative models (e.g., GPT)

- **Text Summarization**
  - **Extractive**: selects original sentences
  - **Abstractive**: generates new text

- **Text Generation**
  - Large language models (e.g., GPT, Claude, Gemini)

- **Multimodal NLP**
  - Text + vision models (e.g., CLIP, GPT-4V)
  - Referred to as “NLP+”

---

## 3. Challenges in NLP

### 3.1 Linguistic Challenges

- **Polysemy (Homonymy)**  
  One word, multiple meanings  
  - *“bank”* (river bank vs. financial bank)

- **Synonymy**  
  Multiple words, same meaning  
  - *sneakers / tennis shoes / running shoes*

- **Context Dependency**
  Observations are not independent.
  - “The dog ate the bone. It tasted good.”  
    → What does “it” refer to?

- **Semantic Ambiguity**
  - “I saw the boy on the beach with my binoculars.”

- **Slang and Colloquialisms**
  - “That jump was sick.”

- **Acronyms**

- **Variable-Length Sequences**
  - Sentences and documents vary in length.

- **Sarcasm and Humor**
  - Difficult for literal models to interpret.

---

## 4. Text Representation

### 4.1 One-Hot Encoding

- Vocabulary size = \( V \)
- Each word → vector of length \( V \)
- Exactly one position = 1, others = 0

Example:
"cat" → [0,0,1,0,...,0]


**Problems:**
- Extremely high-dimensional and sparse
- No semantic similarity captured
- “cat” as different from “kitten” as from “nuclear”

---

## 5. Traditional NLP Methods

### 5.1 Bag of Words (BoW)

- Represents document as word frequency vector
- Ignores grammar and word order
- Vocabulary = all unique words in corpus

Example:
"the cat sat" → {the:1, cat:1, sat:1}


**Limitations:**
- Order ignored
- Sparse representation
- Overemphasizes common words

---

### 5.2 TF-IDF (Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency)

Improves upon BoW by down-weighting common words.

#### Term Frequency (TF)
\[
TF(t,d) = \frac{\text{count of } t \text{ in } d}{\text{total words in } d}
\]

#### Inverse Document Frequency (IDF)
\[
IDF(t) = \log\left(\frac{N}{df_t}\right)
\]

- \( N \) = total documents
- \( df_t \) = documents containing term \( t \)

#### TF-IDF Score
\[
TF\text{-}IDF(t,d) = TF(t,d) \times IDF(t)
\]

**Intuition:**
- Common words → low IDF → low weight
- Rare but document-specific words → high weight

---

### 5.3 N-grams

Capture local word order.

- **Unigram**: 1 word
- **Bigram**: 2 consecutive words
- **Trigram**: 3 consecutive words

Example:
- "machine learning is cool"
- Bigrams: [machine learning], [learning is], [is cool]


Advantages:
- Captures local context
- Distinguishes “not good” from “good”

Limitations:
- Vocabulary explosion
- Increased sparsity

---

### 5.4 Cosine Similarity for Retrieval

Used in classical document retrieval.

\[
\text{cosine similarity} = \frac{A \cdot B}{||A|| \, ||B||}
\]

- 1 → identical
- 0 → orthogonal

Used in TF-IDF-based retrieval systems (precursor to neural retrieval).

---

## 6. Text Preprocessing Pipeline

### Recommended Order

1. **Lowercasing**
2. **Punctuation removal**
3. **Tokenization**
4. **Stopword removal**
5. **Stemming or Lemmatization**

---

### 6.1 Tokenization

Splitting text into units.

#### Word-level
"I love NLP" → ["I", "love", "NLP"]
- Simple
- Struggles with out-of-vocabulary (OOV)

#### Subword (e.g., BPE)
"unhappiness" → ["un", "happy", "ness"]

- Handles OOV
- Used in GPT and BERT

#### Character-level
["I"," ","l","o","v","e"]

- Robust
- Long sequences, limited semantics

---

### 6.2 Stopwords

Common words with low semantic content:
- the, is, a, of, and, etc.

**Caution:**  
Removing stopwords may alter meaning:
"not good" → remove "not" → "good"


---

### 6.3 Stemming vs. Lemmatization

| Method | Description | Output Quality | Speed |
|--------|------------|---------------|--------|
| **Stemming** | Rule-based suffix removal | May produce non-words | Fast |
| **Lemmatization** | Dictionary-based normalization | Real words | Slower |

Examples:
- running → run
- studies → study
- better → good (lemmatization only)

---

## 7. Word Embeddings

### Motivation
One-hot vectors do not encode meaning.

Goal:
- Map words into **dense, low-dimensional vectors**
- Similar words → similar vectors

---

### 7.1 Word2Vec (2013, Mikolov et al.)

Shallow neural network with one hidden layer.

#### Two Architectures

**1. CBOW (Continuous Bag of Words)**
- Context → predict center word
- Faster
- Better for frequent words

**2. Skip-gram**
- Center word → predict context
- Better for rare words

---

### Word2Vec Properties

- Dense embeddings (100–300 dimensions typical)
- Captures semantic relationships
- Enables vector arithmetic:

\[
king - man + woman \approx queen
\]

- **Static embeddings**  
  Same vector regardless of context.

Limitation:
- “bank” has identical embedding in all contexts.

---

### 7.2 GloVe (2014)

- Uses global co-occurrence matrix
- Matrix factorization approach
- Combines global and local statistics
- Static embeddings

---

### 7.3 FastText (2016)

- Extends Word2Vec
- Uses character n-grams
- Handles OOV words
- Effective for morphologically rich languages
- Static embeddings

---

## 8. Sequence Models

Traditional models ignore order. Sequence models capture dependencies.

---

### 8.1 Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs)

Hidden state update:

\[
h_t = \tanh(W_x x_t + W_h h_{t-1} + b)
\]

- Processes tokens sequentially
- Suffers from **vanishing gradient problem**

---

### 8.2 LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory)

Introduces:
- **Cell state**
- **Forget gate**
- **Input gate**
- **Output gate**

Additive memory updates allow gradients to flow over long sequences.

Advantages:
- Handles long-term dependencies better than vanilla RNN.

Limitations:
- Sequential computation (not parallelizable)
- Slow training

---

### 8.3 GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit)

- Simplified LSTM
- Two gates:
  - Update gate
  - Reset gate
- No separate cell state

Often:
- Comparable performance to LSTM
- Fewer parameters

---

## 9. Limitations of RNN-Based Models

- Slow (sequential processing)
- Difficult hyperparameter tuning
- Struggle with very long sequences
- Cannot fully capture long-range dependencies

These limitations motivate **Transformers**, which use self-attention (covered next week).

---

## 10. Implementation Considerations

### 10.1 Handling Variable-Length Sequences

Neural networks require fixed-size tensors.

#### Padding
- Add `<PAD>` tokens
- Use padding masks to ignore during training

#### Packed Sequences (PyTorch)
- Avoid unnecessary computation on padded tokens

---

### 10.2 Data Augmentation for Text

Techniques:
- Back-translation
- Synonym replacement
- Random insertion/deletion
- Random word swapping

Challenges:
- Small changes can alter meaning
- Must preserve label integrity

---

### 10.3 Handling Imbalanced Data

Approaches:
- Oversampling minority class
- Undersampling majority class
- Class-weighted cross-entropy loss
- SMOTE (with embeddings)
- Two-stage training
- Ensemble methods

---

### 10.4 Data Splitting Best Practices

Avoid data leakage.

- Chronological splits for temporal data
- Split conversation threads as units
- Avoid duplicate documents across splits
- Maintain domain consistency

---

## 11. Transfer Learning and Fine-Tuning

Strategies:

- **Full Fine-Tuning**
  - Update all parameters

- **Frozen Backbone**
  - Train only task-specific layers

- **Partial Freezing**
  - Freeze lower layers

- **Gradual Unfreezing**
  - Unfreeze layers progressively during training

---

## 12. NLP Libraries

### NLTK
- Educational
- Tokenization, stemming, corpora access

### spaCy
- Industrial-grade NLP
- Efficient tokenization, NER, parsing

### HuggingFace Transformers
- Pretrained models (BERT, GPT, T5)
- PyTorch and TensorFlow support
- State-of-the-art architectures

---

## 13. Historical Progression of NLP Methods
- BoW → TF-IDF → N-grams → Word2Vec/GloVe/FastText →
- RNN/LSTM/GRU → Transformers → Large Language Models


---

## 14. Key Definitions

- **Polysemy**: One word, multiple meanings  
- **Synonymy**: Multiple words, same meaning  
- **Tokenization**: Splitting text into units  
- **Stemming**: Rule-based word root extraction  
- **Lemmatization**: Dictionary-based normalization  
- **TF-IDF**: Frequency × inverse document rarity  
- **Static Embedding**: Same vector in all contexts  
- **Contextual Embedding**: Vector depends on surrounding words  

---

## 15. Summary

This lecture introduced:

- Core NLP tasks and challenges
- Text preprocessing techniques
- Traditional vectorization methods (BoW, TF-IDF, N-grams)
- Static word embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText)
- Sequence models (RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs)
- Practical NLP implementation considerations

The key limitation of earlier methods is their inability to fully capture context and long-range dependencies — a problem addressed by **Transformers**, which form the foundation of modern large language models.

Next topic: **Attention and Transformer Architectures**.

Outcomes vs. Outputs
Refers to the desired business impact on your organization or for your customer
Stated in terms of the expected impact (which is often $)
Does NOT contain model performance metrics or other technical metrics

Output
Refers to the desired output from the model
Measured in terms of a model performance metric
Typically not communicated to the customer
Set this AFTER setting the desired outcome
Outcomes vs. Outputs
A tool to predict turbulence for airlines
Output
Outcome
Low # of safety incidents per year, or lower $ of safety-related claims
AUROC or precision/recall of turbulence prediction (binary or 1-5 scale)
A power demand forecasting tool for a utility
Lower cost per MWh of power produced
Lower emissions rate per MWh

Baselines
Metrics are meaningless without a baseline for comparison
There are a few important baselines to determine:
Zero rule baseline (Most common class / mean value)
Heuristic baseline
Human baseline
Existing solution baseline
Regression Error Metrics
MSE, MAE and MAPE
Also influenced by scale
More robust to outliers
Can be easier to interpret in context of the problem
Abs value is less desirable for calculations (squared terms are easier to minimize via differentiation)
Mean Absolute Error
Mean Squared Error
Most popular regression error metric
Heavily influenced by outliers - penalizes large errors much more than small ones
Influenced by scale of data
Sometimes used as RMSE
Converts error to a percentage
Popular among non-technical managers because it is easily understood
Skewed by high % errors for low values of y
Mean Absolute % Error
Example: MAE vs. MSE/RMSE
MSE/RMSE penalizes severe errors much more than MAE
This can be desirable if being off by a lot one time is much worse than being off by a little every time
Image source: https://medium.com/human-in-a-machine-world/mae-and-rmse-which-metric-is-better-e60ac3bde13d
Coefficient of determination (R2)
Deviation of points from mean can be broken down into two components:
”Explained deviation” – portion of deviation predicted by your model
“Unexplained deviation” – difference between prediction and actual point
Coefficient of determination (R2)
R2 ranges between 0 and 1
Unexplained deviation (error)
Deviation explained by model
Total deviation from mean
R-squared is typically used to communicate how well your feature variables (X) explain the variability in your target variable (y)
Adjusted R2
R-squared is often viewed as a measure of goodness of fit rather than prediction ability -> calculated “in-sample” on the training data itself
As we add more features, the R-squared almost always goes up because the model finds additional patterns of correlation (which might be noise)
However, this does not mean the model can generate better predictions on new data -> remember our discussion on overfitting
To help with this problem, we often report ”adjusted R-squared”, which penalizes for more features (added complexity)
“Is R-squared useless?”: https://data.library.virginia.edu/is-r-squared-useless/

# AIPI 520: Modeling Process & Algorithms

## 1. Machine Learning in Context: “Machine Learning That Matters”

A central theme of the course is that **building a model is often the easiest part of machine learning**. True impact requires an end-to-end process:

> It is easy to run an algorithm on downloaded data.  
> It is hard to identify the right problem, collect appropriate data, select features, choose methods, evaluate properly, interpret results, and drive adoption.

### Key Stages of ML That Matter
- **Problem identification**
- **Data collection and preprocessing**
- **Feature selection and engineering**
- **Algorithm selection**
- **Evaluation and validation**
- **Interpretation and communication**
- **Deployment and user adoption**

The course emphasizes a **holistic, process-driven approach**, not just algorithm mechanics.

---

## 2. What is Machine Learning?

### Definition
Arthur Samuel (1959):
> Machine learning is the field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed.

### Learning in ML
- **Task-based learning**: Building expertise at a specific task.
- **Generalization**: Transferring learned patterns to new, unseen data.

### Why Use Machine Learning?

ML is appropriate when:

- Automation provides benefit (faster, cheaper, better).
- Rules are:
  - Too complex to specify manually.
  - Unknown or poorly understood.
- Traditional software approaches are infeasible.

---

## 3. What is a Model?

A **model** is:

> A useful approximation of a non-random phenomenon.

Mathematically:

\[
y = f(x) + \varepsilon
\]

Where:
- \(x\): Input variables (features)
- \(y\): Output variable (target)
- \(\varepsilon\): Irreducible error (noise)

### Interpretation
- Models **compress knowledge** into parameters.
- All models are wrong; some are useful.
- A model must be:
  - Non-random
  - Useful
  - An approximation

---

## 4. Structured Data

This course focuses primarily on **structured (tabular) data**.

### Terminology

| Concept | Alternative Terms |
|----------|-------------------|
| Observations | Instances, examples |
| Features | Predictors, attributes, independent variables |
| Targets | Labels, response, dependent variable |

Structured data is typically represented as a matrix:
- Rows → Observations
- Columns → Features

---

## 5. Supervised vs. Unsupervised Learning

### Supervised Learning
- Have features \(X\) and targets \(Y\)
- Learn mapping \(f: X \rightarrow Y\)

Types:
- **Regression** → Numeric output
- **Classification** → Categorical output

### Unsupervised Learning
- Only features \(X\)
- No labeled target
- Goal: Discover structure (e.g., clustering)

### Important Insight
Some problems can be formulated as either regression or classification depending on business requirements.

---

## 6. Heuristics vs. Machine Learning

### Heuristics
- Rule-based systems
- Hard-coded decision logic
- Example: Recommend most popular item

Benefits:
- Easy to build
- Low computational cost
- High interpretability

### Machine Learning
- Learns patterns from data
- Adaptive (can retrain)
- Handles complex relationships

### Best Practice
Always begin with:
1. **Heuristic baseline**
2. **Simple ML baseline**
3. Then increase complexity if justified

---

## 7. Algorithm Selection

### No Free Lunch Theorem
No single algorithm is best for all problems.

### Three Key Criteria

1. **Performance**
2. **Interpretability**
3. **Computational cost**

### Occam’s Razor
> All else equal, choose the simpler model.

Simple models:
- Easier to maintain
- More robust to drift
- Often generalize better
- May perform as well as complex models

Industry often prioritizes:
- Practicality
- Maintainability
- Interpretability

---

## 8. Model Evaluation

### Train-Test Split

Purpose: Estimate generalization performance.

Typical split:
- 80–90% Training
- 10–20% Test

**Never tune models on the test set.**

---

## 9. Sampling

### Why Sample?
- Limited access to full population
- Computational constraints

### Types of Sampling

#### Non-probability Sampling
- Convenience sampling
- Snowball sampling
- Judgment sampling
- Quota sampling

Risk:
- Bias
- Poor generalization

#### Random Sampling
- Simple random sampling
- Stratified sampling
- Weighted sampling

Stratified sampling is crucial for:
- Class imbalance

---

## 10. Data Leakage

**Data leakage occurs when test information influences training.**

Common causes:
- Feature selection before splitting
- Scaling before splitting
- Imputation before splitting
- Duplicate records across splits
- Random splitting of time series
- Group leakage (e.g., same patient in train/test)

### Rule:
> Split first. Preprocess second.

---

## 11. Validation & Cross-Validation

### Three-Way Split
- Training
- Validation
- Test

### K-Fold Cross-Validation
- Divide into \(K\) folds
- Train on \(K-1\), validate on remaining
- Average validation error

Benefits:
- Better generalization estimate
- Efficient use of small datasets

Variants:
- ShuffleSplit
- Leave-One-Out (LOOCV)

After CV:
- Final evaluation must still use test set.

---

## 12. Bias–Variance Tradeoff

Total error consists of:

\[
\text{Error} = \text{Bias}^2 + \text{Variance} + \text{Irreducible Error}
\]

### Bias
- Error from overly simple assumptions
- Underfitting

### Variance
- Sensitivity to training data noise
- Overfitting

### Optimal Model
Found at balance point between bias and variance.

### Overfitting Pattern
- Training performance ↑
- Validation performance peaks then ↓
- Divergence indicates overfitting

Model complexity influenced by:
- Algorithm choice
- Number of features
- Hyperparameters
- Dataset size

---

## 13. Metrics: Outcomes vs. Outputs

### Outcome
- Business goal
- Measured in impact (e.g., cost reduction)

### Output
- Model performance metric
- Technical measure

Example:

| Problem | Outcome | Output |
|----------|----------|----------|
| Turbulence prediction | Fewer safety incidents | AUROC |
| Power demand forecasting | Lower cost per MWh | MSE |

**Define outcome first. Then choose metric.**

---

## 14. Regression Metrics

### Mean Squared Error (MSE)

\[
MSE = \frac{1}{n}\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
\]

- Penalizes large errors heavily
- Scale dependent
- Differentiable

### Mean Absolute Error (MAE)

\[
MAE = \frac{1}{n}\sum |y_i - \hat{y}_i|
\]

- More robust to outliers
- Easier interpretation

### Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE)

\[
MAPE = \frac{100}{n}\sum \left|\frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{y_i}\right|
\]

- Interpretable
- Problematic when \(y\) near zero

### R² (Coefficient of Determination)

\[
R^2 = \frac{\text{Explained Variance}}{\text{Total Variance}}
\]

Ranges:
- 0 to 1

### Adjusted R²
Penalizes additional features to account for overfitting.

---

## 15. Classification Metrics

Accuracy may be misleading under class imbalance.

Important metrics:
- Precision
- Recall
- False Positive Rate
- AUROC
- Precision-Recall curve

Metric choice depends on:
- Business objective
- Cost of false positives vs false negatives

---

## 16. Course Philosophy & Real-World Emphasis

The course emphasizes:

- Structured problem framing
- Real-world messy data
- Interpretability
- Practical deployment concerns
- Critical thinking beyond coding

In an era where AI automates execution:
- Programming is necessary but not sufficient.
- Planning, evaluation, and reasoning matter more.
- Understanding tradeoffs is essential.

---

# Core Takeaways

- ML is a **process**, not just an algorithm.
- Always establish a **baseline**.
- Prefer **simpler models** when adequate.
- Guard against **data leakage**.
- Use **cross-validation** properly.
- Understand the **bias-variance tradeoff**.
- Align model metrics with **business outcomes**.
- Evaluate models in context, not in isolation.

Why do we sample?
We don’t have access to all possible data

Sampling occurs at multiple points
Sampling from the entire population to create training data
Sampling from the training data to create a test set
Sampling from the training data to do quick experiments
Two main types of sampling: nonprobability sampling and random sampling
Nonprobability sampling
Nonprobability sampling is when the selection of data is not based on any probability criteria
Types of nonprobability sampling:
Convenience sampling – samples selected based on their availability
E.g. Use Google Image Search for pictures of flowers to train on
Snowball sampling – Future samples selected based on existing samples
E.g. scraping Twitter accounts based on users you follow
Judgment sampling – Domain experts decide what samples to use
Quota sampling – Select samples based on quotas for sub-groups
E.g. a survey where you collect 100 responses from users of each age group
Nonprobability sampling
Samples are not representative of real-world data and thus are highly likely to cause bias in your model
However, this is a very common approach in practice
Examples:
Large language models are trained on easily collected data – Wikipedia, Reddit, Common Crawl etc
Sentiment analysis models often trained on IMDB movie reviews or Amazon reviews – biased towards people who leave reviews online
Self-driving cars – initially trained only on Phoenix, AZ and Bay Area.  Waymo later expanded to include Kirkland, WA for rainy weather
Random sampling
Random sampling involves randomly choosing samples from population
Several types:
Simple random sampling – all samples have equal probability of being selected
Downside – certain rare categories may not appear in the sampled data
Stratified sampling – divide population into groups you care about and sample a % randomly from each group
One challenge is that some observations may fall into multiple groups
Weighted sampling – each sample is given a weight which determines the probability of being selected
Allows you to apply domain expertise in selection e.g. weight recent data higher
Helps when your available data has a different distribution than the true data
Sampling for test set
Take a random sample of indices to use for test set, use remainder for training
Use Scikit-learn’s train_test_split method

Data Leakage
“Data leakage” occurs when some of our test set data “leaks” into model building and influences the development of the model
For example, if we use all of our data to select our features, or compare algorithms
This invalidates the estimated performance of the model and causes it to be overoptimistic
In severe cases, it can cause our model to be worthless
Data Leakage
Data from the future is accidentally used within training data
Data Leakage
A variable within the training data is an indicator of the target
Common causes of data leakage
Selecting features before splitting

Filling missing values before splitting
Grouped observations are separated into different splits
E.g. two CT scans from the same patient taken a week apart
Not great

Particularly dangerous when merging multiple datasets together

A Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve plots the True Positive Rate (TPR) and False Positive Rate (FPR) for different threshold values
What is a threshold?
Most classification models return the probability of the positive class
The data scientist sets a threshold for the positive class – if the probability returned by the model is above threshold, the assigned label is positive

A common error metric for classification models is AUROC
This represents the area under the ROC curve
A perfect classifier will have have AUROC=1
A random classifier will have AUROC=0.5
Why? See: https://datascience.stackexchange.com/questions/31872/auc-roc-of-a-random-classifier
Therefore, a model should have an AUROC between 0.5 and 1 (higher is better)

This measures the tradeoff between recall and precision as the model threshold is varied (just like we did for the ROC)

We are NOT trying to select the optimal combination for modeling
Two objectives:
Remove features which have very little to contribute in predicting the response (e.g. features with no/low correlation to the output)

Select a user-specified number of features which score highest on a univariate statistical test
Inputs: features (X), response (y), number to select (k), statistical test (score-func)

Embedded Methods – Random Forest
We can calculate the relative importance of each feature using the random forest’s model.feature_importances_ attribute
“Feature importance” is calculated by looking at how much the nodes that use each feature reduce gini impurity on average (across each tree and then all trees in the forest), weighted by number of samples at node
Feature selection strategy

Working with Categorical Features
Continuous vs categorical features
Continuous
Numeric variable that has an infinite number of values between any two values
E.g. length of a part, temperature, height, time
Categorical
Finite number of categories / distinct groups
May or may not have a logical order
E.g. gender, student major, material type, color
Discrete
Numeric variable that has a countable number of values between two values
E.g. age, number of parts, year made
Rule of thumb – if number of possible values small, treat as categorical
Encoding categorical features
Many machine learning models are algebraic and only know how to accept numerical inputs
We need to convert our categorical (string) features into number codes
Two ways to do this:
Numerical (ordinal) encoding
One-hot encoding
Example – predicting health insurance claims
Objective is to predict the total medical claims of customers of a health insurance company based on demographic data
Features:
Sex – categorical
Age_group – categorical
Body Mass Index (BMI) - continuous
Children - continuous
Smoker – categorical (binary)
Region – categorical
Response:
Charges - continuous
How should we handle the categorical variables?
Method 1: Ordinal encoding
For ordered data there is value in preserving the ordering (e.g. education level, class grade)
Converts ordinal categories to numerical codes
Can also use for non-ordered data (but creates risk that model will learn artificial relationships)
Method 2: One-hot encoding
Each categorical variable with n categories is split into n different binary features (0/1)
Scaling/Standardizing
Why scale/standardize your data?
Some distance-based models (e.g. clustering or K Nearest Neighbors) will only work when features are on the same scale
E.g. trying to compare two people using the dimensions “Age” and “Household Income” via a distance metric such as Euclidian distance will not be useful
Other machine learning models may converge faster/better (e.g. logistic regression, neural networks)
Improves interpretability of models results (e.g. can directly compare coefficients of a regression model and interpret intercept)
Scaling vs. Standardizing
Min-Max Scaling (Normalization)
Change the values for each feature so they fall in a fixed range – usually 0 to 1
Commonly used for computer vision applications (scaling pixel values to 0–255)
Used when data distribution is not approximately normal
May diminish the impact of outliers
Standardization
(Z-score normalization)
Change the values for each feature so they have properties of a standard normal distribution with μ=0 and σ=1
Important for clustering analysis and PCA, helps neural networks
May distort differences between features if not approximately normally distributed
Scikit learn: MinMaxScaler()
Scikit learn: StandardScaler()
Rules of Thumb
Some algorithms require either scaling or standardizing
Distance-based algorithms such as KNN, clustering
Regression with L1/L2 penalty
Some (e.g. PCA) require standardizing
It never hurts to scale/standardize, and even if not required it often helps improve convergence
Class Imbalance
Bias from class imbalance
“Class imbalance” means that one label class is significantly more common in the training dataset than others
Class imbalance may be inherent in the phenomenon being modeled:
Car insurance claims
Financial fraud
Side effects of new medicine
It may also be introduced through sampling bias in building the training dataset:
IBM’s facial recognition software
Amazon’s AI-based resume screening system
Why does class imbalance matter?
The model learns that if it predicts the majority class more, it will perform better
As a result, it’s ability to predict the minority class when it occurs is impaired
Selection of metrics can make this worse
E.g. if we use a simple metric like “accuracy”, we could convince ourselves we have a great model if it predicts a “0” 100% of the time!
Dealing with class imbalance
If the class imbalance is a result of bias in collecting training data, fix the root problem by collecting more data
If the imbalance is inherent in the problem, two common techniques uses are undersampling the majority class, and oversampling the minority class
https://www.kaggle.com/rafjaa/resampling-strategies-for-imbalanced-datasets
